Unlike sort-free Gaussian Splatting methods (e.g., LC-WSR) which lack early termination due to their design, ET enables significant speedups comparable to vanilla 3DGS without requiring an explicit Gaussian order [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and passages that 'Unlike prior sort-free Gaussian Splatting methods (e.g., LC-WSR) which lack early termination due to their sort-free design, Duplex-GS achieves termination results comparable to vanilla 3DGS without requiring an explicit Gaussian order.' It further confirms that the early termination mechanism enables significant acceleration ('offers a solution for resource-constrained platform for its significant acceleration') and that the threshold is maintained at the same value as vanilla 3DGS. All components of the claim are directly supported by the provided text.
supported
The method relies on physically grounded transmittance to eliminate transparency artifacts and enable early termination without explicit sorting [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in Section VI.2 that 'The physically grounded transmittance... is the key innovation which eliminates transparency artifacts as well as enable early termination.' Furthermore, Section VI.3 and the notes confirm that this mechanism allows for early termination (halting blending when transmittance drops below a threshold) and that it works 'without requiring an explicit Gaussian order' (sort-free), unlike prior methods like LC-WSR. Thus, all parts of the claim are directly supported by the text.

The cell-level transmittance $T_{\text{cell}}^n$ is the key innovation that eliminates transparency artifacts and enables early termination [S1].

The claim is directly supported by the text in Source [S1]. Specifically, Section '2) Cell-level Transmittance' explicitly states: 'The physically grounded transmittance, shown in Eq. 16, is the key innovation which eliminates transparency artifacts as well as enable early termination.' Additionally, the notes and passages confirm that this mechanism allows for early termination by halting blending when transmittance decays below a threshold, thereby eliminating transparency artifacts.
supported

A rendering optimization that halts the front-to-back blending process at the cell level once the cell-level transmittance decays below a predefined threshold $\epsilon$, eliminating transparency artifacts and accelerating rendering [S1].

The claim states that the optimization halts front-to-back blending at the cell level when cell-level transmittance decays below a threshold epsilon, which eliminates transparency artifacts and accelerates rendering. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section B ('Early Termination for Cell Based 3DGS'), stating: 'the cell-level transmittance T cell n decays towards zero during front-to-back rendering, eliminating transparency artifacts. This provides a natural mechanism for early termination: the blending process is halted in cell level once T cell n falls below a predefined threshold ϵ... This approach effectively accelerates rendering.' Additionally, Section VI.2 confirms that physically grounded transmittance 'eliminates transparency artifacts as well as enable early termination.' All specific details in the claim are present and supported by the evidence.
supported

Early Termination (ET) is an acceleration mechanism for Gaussian Splatting that selectively omits computations for Gaussians with negligible impact on the final rendered output [S1].

The claim states that Early Termination (ET) is an acceleration mechanism for Gaussian Splatting that selectively omits computations for Gaussians with negligible impact on the final rendered output. Source [S1] explicitly defines ET in Section VI.2 and VI.3, stating that it 'selectively omit computations that have negligible impact on the final rendered output with extremely small transmittance' and that 'This approach effectively accelerates rendering.' The evidence directly supports every part of the claim.

If the opacity parameters are not constrained to physically plausible ranges (e.g., $[0, 1]$), the transmittance may not decay correctly, leading to artifacts or failure to terminate [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the proposed formulation constrains the opacity parameter to the physically plausible range of [0, 1]. It further notes that without these physical constraints (as in prior methods like LC-WSR), the method suffers from 'transparency artifacts' and lacks the 'physically grounded transmittance' that allows for early termination. The text links the physical plausibility of opacity directly to the ability of transmittance to decay correctly (towards zero), which enables the early termination mechanism. Therefore, the claim that unconstrained opacity leads to incorrect decay, artifacts, or failure to terminate is supported by the evidence.
